title: The wild world of modern penis enlargement | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

When Daniel Lombroso set about making “Manhood,” a documentary film tracing the meteoric rise of a new penile girth enhancement product in the US, he wasn’t sure if men would want to talk. There were teens aged 18 and 19 years old as well as men in their 70s, 80s and 90s. Most were straight, which surprised Lombroso. But “believe it or not, our success rate was pretty high,” he said in a video call from New York. Around half of the guys he met at a clinic in Dallas were willing to participate in his film — some comfortable showing their face but not their penis, others wanting the camera on their penis but not their face. At least one, he said, was more out-and-out proud: “I still get dick pics to this day.”

The filmmaker and video journalist has spent the last three years investigating the popularity of Phallofill, a trademarked injectable procedure developed byTexan aesthetics practitioner Bill Moore. For weeks, Lombroso sat in Moore’s waiting room observing the stream of guys filter in to have their genitals enlarged with hyaluronic acid filler — the same substance at the center of this year’s Winter Olympics“penis-gate,”after a German newspaper alleged ski jumpers were using it to improve aerodynamics.

The film shows us how this ancient male anxiety is being re-animated by the modern context of so-called “lunchtime” injectable filler. “I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged, a border patrol agent, a father of five, a brain cancer survivor, an OnlyFans star,” he said. “It felt like this incredible, unexpected portrait across America.”

Men are now one of the fastest growing demographics for plastic surgery in the US, according to the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.Facelifts and facial fat grafts saw a bigger increase in male patients in 2025 compared with female patients. Some surgeries, such as Brazilian butt lifts and rhinoplasties, saw a rise in male patients even when the number of female patients dipped. “I think men are finally grappling with their own body dysmorphia, their own insecurities, the ways that they want to modify their appearance for the first time,” Lombroso said.

Prescriptions for finasteride in the US, a popular hair regrowth medication, increased 200% between 2017 and 2024.Just last month, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. decided to make non-US Food and Drug Administration approved peptides touted by online influencers for weight loss, muscle building and longevity available through compounding pharmaciesacross the country. “The film is not pro penis enlargement. It’s not anti penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore this well of male insecurity that pervades so much of what we do, from the cultural level all the way to the political level,” Lombroso said.

A central character of Lombroso’s film is Ruben, a Mexican Americanmiddle-aged father-of-five who works 12-hour-shifts to support his single-income household. Yet despite living on a hamster wheel of debt, Ruben was paying thousands per penis enlargement session with Moore. Over the course of the film, the financial pressure mounts, but his injections continue — even when Ruben’s partner Lana expresses complete disinterest and the family end up moving out of their home. It’s a baffling scenario made more legible when we learn about Ruben’s childhood sexual trauma, and observing what Lombroso calls the “passive noise” of his life: the manospheric podcasts we watch him absorb in the shower, while he drives and even when he’s eating dinner with his family. “These are podcasts that are telling you all the time that the way to be strong is to have a bigger penis, get a nicer car or who knows what, eat more elk meat,” he said. “Then here comes these practitioners on your feed that say, ‘I have a solution. I can cure your depression. I can help you get a promotion. You might become a CEO.’ ”

Moore has built an empire promising men not only more inches, but access to some elusive charisma and power. “There definitely is something to the BDE, the Big Dick Energy,” Moore says in the film. “Everytime I call him, he’s busier, he’s in more locations,” said Lombroso. “And that’s only going to grow from there.” The documentary also shows urologistsupskilling in Phallofill administration — something that concerned Lombroso. He thought many were pivoting away from “important work” with erectile dysfunction solutions to “basically Botox injections in your penis, because they see dollar signs.”

As it turns out, the story of penis enlargement has many of the disparate threads that make up so much of our contemporary despair: financial insecurity, the loneliness of the digital world, loud polarizing media, the easy accessibility of cosmetic surgery.But at the heart of the documentary is empathy. “These men are a marketplace, and millions of dollars can be made off of them,” Lombroso said. “Usually the problem isn’t your penis. Usually the problem is a lot deeper.”
